attempts.label: DANDI:000007
attempts.paper_title: A cortico-cerebellar loop for motor planning
attempts.entry_title: A cortico-cerebellar loop for motor planning (Gao et al. 2018)
attempts.summary: In this data the paper's central ALM findings held up: fastigial photo-activation during the delay caused errors and collapsed ALM preparatory activity along its coding direction, and photo-inhibiting the cerebellar nuclei abolished late-delay ALM selectivity. The recordings from the cerebellar nuclei, the lesions, licking and the anatomy could not be tested, as the dataset holds only the ALM sessions. That ALM recovers after dentate photo-activation did not reproduce, as a few percent of neurons stayed altered more than 1 s later. Counts of modulated neurons and firing rate levels mostly missed, as the files hold more neurons than the paper reports and do not say which it excluded.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Gao, Davis, Thomas, Economo, Abrego, Svoboda, De Zeeuw and Li (2018) that can be tested on dandiset 000007, which holds the ALM recordings of 13 mice during CN photo-activation or photo-inhibition. It tests ALM selectivity, the effects of CN photostimulation on ALM neurons and on the coding direction, and the behavior of the recording sessions. The lesion, CN recording, licking, VGAT-ChR2 and anatomy data are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Gao et al. (2018) from dandiset 000007

outcomes.statement: Fastigial nucleus lesions impair contralesional licking choices, measured as lower performance on trials instructing contralesional licking after the lesion than before.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1d
outcomes.quote: Fastigial lesions impaired initiation of contralesional licking ( Fig 1d )

statistics.test: one-sided bootstrap, pre- versus post lesion

outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); the 8 lesion mice (AN098 to AN104, CD05, NL13) and any pre- and post-lesion sessions are not in it. Checked the archive's asset list and every file's subject and trials table.

outcomes.statement: After fastigial lesion, the first lick to the contralesional side comes later after the go cue than the first lick to the ipsilesional side, while lick rate within bouts and bout duration are unchanged.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1e; Extended Data Figure 1b and 1c
outcomes.quote: slowed initiation of contralesional licking following the 'go' cue ( Fig 1e ). After movement initiation licking was unaffected

statistics.about: time of first lick, contralesional against ipsilesional

outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); no lesion mice, and the files hold no lick times, so neither reaction time nor lick bouts can be computed.

outcomes.statement: Dentate nucleus lesions do not change behavioral choice or movement execution.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 2; Figure 1d
outcomes.quote: Dentate lesions (~1.5 mm away) did not change behavioral choice and movement execution
outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); the dentate lesion mice are not in it.

outcomes.statement: Fastigial photo-activation during the early sample epoch does not affect behavioral choice for either trial type.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Fastigial photo-activation during the early sample epoch had no effect on behavioral choice (p>0.05 for either trial type, bootstrap, Methods)
outcomes.notes: Code 1 (early sample photo-activation) in the 6 fastigial mice, 21 sessions. Contra trials 0.903 control against 0.916 photo-activation (one-sided bootstrap p = 0.31), ipsi 0.842 against 0.824 (p = 0.41), pooled 0.873 against 0.867 (p = 0.45).
deviations: The photostimulation codes are not described in the files; codes 1 and 3 are read as early sample and 2 and 4 as early delay photo-activation, 5 and 6 as delay photo-inhibition, from the onset of the ALM response and the sessions' ogen sites (data check).
Tested on the ALM recording sessions, the only behavior in the dataset; the paper's behavior may include other sessions.

outcomes.statement: Fastigial photo-activation during the early delay epoch lowers behavioral performance, even though the photostimulus ends 800 ms before the movement.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 1g
outcomes.quote: Photo-activation during the delay and response epochs both resulted in incorrect choices ( Fig 1g–h ). Incorrect choices were induced even when the photostimuli ceased 800 ms before the movement
outcomes.notes: Code 2 (early delay photo-activation), 6 mice, 21 sessions, 3715 control and 446 photo-activation trials. Performance 0.873 against 0.630 (change -0.243), no resample of 10,000 with a non-negative change (p < 0.0001). Every mouse drops (0.447 to 0.782 against 0.745 to 0.921). The 800 ms gap to the movement holds by design (0.455 s stimulus from delay onset, 1.3 s delay).
deviations: The photostimulation codes are not described in the files; codes 1 and 3 are read as early sample and 2 and 4 as early delay photo-activation, 5 and 6 as delay photo-inhibition, from the onset of the ALM response and the sessions' ogen sites (data check).
Tested on the ALM recording sessions, the only behavior in the dataset; the paper's behavior may include other sessions.

outcomes.statement: Fastigial photo-activation during the delay epoch biases future movements toward either the contralateral or the ipsilateral direction, depending on the mouse.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 1h; Extended Data Figure 1e
outcomes.quote: Photo-activation during the delay epoch biased future movements to either the contralateral or ipsilateral direction in individual mice
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), early delay, the only one in the dataset. Contra-bias mice anm00314746 (contra drop 0.200, p = 0.023) and anm00314757 (0.331, p = 0.001); ipsi-bias mice BAYLORNL15 (0.411, p < 0.0001), anm00314758 (0.190, p = 0.022), anm00314760 (0.370, p < 0.0001); BAYLORCD6 neither. At p < 0.01, 1 and 2 mice. Contra and ipsi are by instructed direction relative to the files' ogen site, which agrees with Supplemental Table 1 for these mice where both name them.
deviations: The photostimulation codes are not described in the files; codes 1 and 3 are read as early sample and 2 and 4 as early delay photo-activation, 5 and 6 as delay photo-inhibition, from the onset of the ALM response and the sessions' ogen sites (data check).
Tested on the ALM recording sessions, the only behavior in the dataset; the paper's behavior may include other sessions.
Reading (b), the 1.255 s whole delay stimulus, is not in the recording sessions.

outcomes.statement: Fastigial photo-activation during the response epoch produces a contralateral bias, opposite to the bias of fastigial lesions.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 1h
outcomes.quote: Photo-activation immediately before movement onset (response epoch) produced a contralateral bias ( Fig 1h ), opposite from the directional bias induced by fastigial lesions
outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); the recording sessions have photo-activation at sample or delay onset only (codes 1 to 4); there is no response epoch photo-activation.

outcomes.statement: Fastigial photo-activation does not block or change the frequency and duration of licking after a lick bout starts, and photo-activation in the delay does not evoke early licks.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 1i; Extended Data Figure 1f
outcomes.quote: Fastigial photo-activation did not block or perturb the frequency and duration of licking movements after initiation of licking bouts ( Fig 1i ). Fastigial photo-activation during the delay epoch did not evoke early licks
outcomes.notes: The files hold no lick times, so lick rate within bouts and bout duration cannot be computed, and the response epoch photo-activation is not in the dataset. The early lick part alone, shown in the notebook (section Early licks), does not decide the outcome. The early lick fraction is 0.079 in control and 0.127 with delay photo-activation (one-sided p = 0.17, two-sided 0.35), with BAYLORCD6 rising from 0.081 to 0.324. Lick early trials keep their photostimulation code (data check).

outcomes.statement: Dentate photo-activation produces little effect on behavioral choice.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 3; Figure 1g
outcomes.quote: Dentate photo-activation produced little effect on behavioral choice ( Fig 1g , p=0.06, bootstrap
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), early delay (code 4), 3 dentate mice and 13 sessions. Pooled performance 0.873 against 0.835 (change -0.038), one-sided p = 0.108, so no drop at p < 0.05 (paper p = 0.06). Ipsi trials alone drop by 0.063 (p = 0.041), contra by 0.013 (p = 0.45). The outcome rests on 3 of the paper's 8 mice. Without anm00314756 20151023 (clock check) the change is -0.037, p = 0.157. The verifier notes that the hierarchical bootstrap is conservative, which favours a claim of absence such as this one.
deviations: The photostimulation codes are not described in the files; codes 1 and 3 are read as early sample and 2 and 4 as early delay photo-activation, 5 and 6 as delay photo-inhibition, from the onset of the ALM response and the sessions' ogen sites (data check).
Tested on the ALM recording sessions, the only behavior in the dataset; the paper's behavior may include other sessions.
3 of the paper's 8 dentate mice (NL12, NL14 and anm00314756, which is AN106 by its site); reading (b), the 1.255 s stimulus, is not in the dataset.

outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 1k

outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 1k; Extended Data Figure 2g and 2h
outcomes.quote: Photo-inhibition during the late sample and delay epochs resulted in incorrect behavioral choices, with a larger effect induced in the delay epoch

sub-epoch photo-inhibition, the stronger effect marked

outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); the 0.5 s sub-epoch photo-inhibitions of Extended Data Fig. 2h are not in it; the recording sessions hold only the 1.3 s delay photo-inhibition, which lowers pooled performance from 0.848 to 0.693 (shown under fig1k-inhibition-delay-bias).

outcomes.statement: Fastigial photo-inhibition during the delay epoch biases future movements to the contralateral or the ipsilateral direction, depending on the mouse.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Extended Data Figure 2g and 2h
outcomes.quote: Photo-inhibition during the delay epoch biased future movements to either the contralateral or ipsilateral direction in individual mice
outcomes.notes: Reading (b), 1.3 s delay photo-inhibition (codes 5 and 6 pooled), on recording sessions. CD12 and CD13, the two of the paper's three mice (CD12, CD13, CD16) in the dataset, both drop on the same trial type (0.161, p = 0.022, and 0.221, p = 0.015; the other type changes by +0.009 and +0.011): contra by the files' hemispheres, ipsi by Supplemental Table 1, which disagree for these mice. So within the paper's mice only one direction is seen; CD16 is not in the dataset. With CD08 and CD14 (recorded mice not in the paper's 1.3 s behavior set), both directions occur under either hemisphere assignment (3 contra and 1 ipsi, or 1 and 3). Without the four CD12 and CD13 sessions the clock check could not show, CD12 and CD13 still drop on the same trial type (0.170, p = 0.025, and 0.282, p < 0.001).

Tested on the ALM recording sessions, the only behavior in the dataset; the paper's behavior may include other sessions.

outcomes.statement: Fastigial photo-inhibition during the response epoch produces an ipsilateral bias, as fastigial lesions do and opposite to photo-activation.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 1k

outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); there is no response epoch photo-inhibition in the recording sessions.

outcomes.statement: Fastigial photo-inhibition minimally affects movement execution, and at the intensities of the task evokes no consistent movement.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 4; Figure 1l; Extended Data Figure 2e, 2f and 2i; Methods, CN photo-inhibition and effects on movement
outcomes.quote: Photo-inhibition minimally affected movement execution ( Fig 1l ). No other movements were consistently evoked during photo-inhibition
outcomes.notes: The files hold no lick times and no video or jaw tracking (data check lists every group of the files; acquisition and processing are empty); the 6 mice of Extended Data Fig. 2e and 2f are not in the dataset. The early lick part alone, run in the notebook on the 4 L7-cre x Ai32 recording mice (the claim's 7 mice are not in the dataset), shows no change, 0.109 of control trials against 0.117 of delay photo-inhibition trials (two-sided p = 0.59). It does not decide the outcome.

outcomes.statement: In VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, fastigial photostimulation in the early delay reduces performance on both trial types (contra lick 74.5% to 58.5%, ipsi lick 67.8% to 57.0%).
outcomes.source: Methods, ALM photo-inhibition after a fastigial perturbation, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: fastigial perturbations during the early delay epoch reduced behavioral performance for both trial types (control ... 74.5% correct, "ipsi lick" trials, 67.8%; photostimulation ... 58.5% and 57.0%; p<0.05 for both trial types, bootstrap)
outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); the 4 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice (ZD02 to ZD05) are not in it.

outcomes.statement: Most ALM putative pyramidal neurons (980 of 1194) distinguish "lick left" from "lick right" trials in their spike counts.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5; Methods, Electrophysiology data analysis
outcomes.quote: Most ALM pyramidal neurons distinguished "lick left" and "lick right" trials in spike counts (980/1194, p<0.05, two-tailed t-test, Methods)
outcomes.notes: 34 sessions of the 9 photo-activation mice, 1082 putative pyramidal neurons. Selective (E2, control trials) 800 (0.739) with correct trials and a 1.3 s response window, 815 (0.753) with 1.5 s; with all trials 794 (0.734) under both windows, just outside 0.738 to 0.902. Counts reported, not judged, as the dataset holds 9 of 10 mice. Per mouse 0.286 to 0.838; fastigial sessions 0.659, dentate 0.825. With the files' cell_type 0.737 (820 of 1112); with photostimulation trials included 0.766.
deviations: Putative pyramidal neurons by the width of the files' mean waveforms (E1), which gives more neurons than the paper reports; the units table has no quality field to tell which the paper left out.

Lick early trials are left out of the neural analyses (the Methods say so for performance only); a standard choice. So are trials outside the units' observation intervals (120 trials of BAYLORCD8 20171020, which hold no spikes).
The selectivity test uses control trials only; the paper does not say whether photostimulation trials enter (a variant with them gives 0.766).
9 of the paper's 10 mice: the dataset does not hold the mouse whose CN injection missed.

outcomes.statement: A proportion of CN neurons similar to ALM (416 of 564) shows trial-type selectivity.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: A similar proportion of CN neurons showed trial-type selectivity (416/564)
outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); the 878 CN units of 18 mice are not in it.

outcomes.statement: Preparatory activity (selectivity before the response epoch) is more prevalent in ALM (59% of neurons) than in the CN (35%).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: Preparatory activity (selectivity before the response epoch) was more prevalent in ALM (ALM, 59% of neurons, CN, 35%; p<0.001, chi-square test)
outcomes.notes: The comparison needs the CN recordings, which are not in the dataset. ALM alone (notebook, fig2-alm-selective-fraction table) gives 0.525 of all neurons (0.710 of selective) with correct trials and 0.500 (0.681) with all trials, against the paper's 0.59.

outcomes.statement: Peri-movement activity (selectivity in the response epoch) is equally prevalent in ALM (67%) and the CN (66%).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: Peri-movement activity (selectivity during response epoch) was equally prevalent in both regions (ALM, 67%, CN, 66%)
outcomes.notes: The comparison needs the CN recordings, which are not in the dataset. ALM alone gives 0.572 to 0.587 of all neurons and 0.778 to 0.794 of selective neurons, against the paper's 0.67.

outcomes.statement: In both ALM and the CN, a similar small proportion of neurons (under 10%) modulates its spike rate during individual licks.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 5; Extended Data Figure 4a to 4c
outcomes.quote: In both regions, a similar proportion (<10%) of neurons modulated their spike rates during individual licks
outcomes.notes: The files hold no lick times, and the CN recordings are not in the dataset.

outcomes.statement: Selectivity for "lick left" and "lick right" trials emerges gradually in both the ALM and the CN population averages, starting during the sample epoch and peaking in the response epoch.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 6; Figure 2c and 2d
outcomes.quote: Selectivity for "lick left" and "lick right" trials emerged gradually in both ALM and CN population averages ( Fig 2c–d ), starting during the sample epoch and reaching a maximum at the response epoch
outcomes.notes: On ALM (800 selective neurons, 778 or 798 with enough trials), every reading has the population selectivity's interval above zero in 16 to 22 sample-epoch windows and a delay mean above the sample mean (0.66 to 1.76 against 0.22 to 0.60 spikes/s). The maximum lies in the response epoch only when the response epoch fixes the preferred trial type (0.50 s and 0.25 s after the go cue, 2.22 and 2.26 spikes/s); with the sample or delay epoch it is before the go cue (-0.60 to -0.05 s). The paper says the epoch gave similar preparatory activity (Methods, "Selecting preferred trial type using either sample, delay, or response epoch data yielded qualitatively similar preparatory activity"), which holds here, as the sample and delay parts are similar under every epoch; that sentence does not cover the peak's place, which holds under one of the three epochs only. With the neurons selected on one half of the correct control trials and the selectivity measured on the other half (678 selective, 662 with enough trials), the pattern is the same (13 to 22 sample windows above zero; maximum in the response epoch only with the response epoch). The CN half is not in the dataset.
deviations: Putative pyramidal neurons by the width of the files' mean waveforms (E1), which gives more neurons than the paper reports.

Correct control trials (Fig. 2a shows correct trials; Fig. 2c is not a photostimulation analysis); selective neurons by E2 with correct trials and a 1.3 s response window. The maximum is searched to 1.3 s after the go cue.
E3 leaves open whether the 10 preference trials are 10 of each type or 10 in all, and which epoch fixes the preference; all six combinations are run.
Only the ALM half; the CN recordings are not in the dataset.

outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 8; Extended Data Figure 6a to 6e

outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); no CN recordings.

outcomes.statement: CN photo-inhibition during the delay rapidly alters the activity of many ALM neurons (197 of 454), with a latency of 7.1 plus or minus 3.8 ms.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 3d and 3e; Extended Data Figure 5e
outcomes.quote: Activity of many ALM neurons was rapidly altered by CN photo-inhibition (197/454, p<0.01, two-tailed t-test, Extended Data Fig 5e ; latency, 7.1 ± 3.8 ms)
outcomes.notes: 4 L7-cre x Ai32 mice, 20 sessions, 676 putative pyramidal neurons (paper 454 in 19 sessions), outside 454 +/- 45.4. Modulated in the delay epoch 270 with all trials and 223 with correct trials, outside 197 +/- 19.7. The dataset holds more neurons than the paper, so the criterion's fraction, given for fewer neurons, does not apply; the fraction, 0.399, is inside 0.39 to 0.48. Per mouse 0.185 to 0.525. Latency (E5), bootstrap mean 14.37, 17.09 and 21.29 ms by bin start, centre and end (all trials; correct trials 14.05 to 22.33), against 7.1 +/- 3.8 ms, with bootstrap s.d. 11.5 to 14.7 ms; observed onsets 24 to 37 ms; 14.55 to 32.52 ms with the pre-onset change subtracted. By code, the population change is significant from the bins starting 30 ms (code 5) and 32 ms (code 6) after delay onset, against 4 ms for fastigial photo-activation. Code 6 also has a small significant change in the bins starting -2 to 2 ms, gone by 4 ms. The files hold no laser trace, so a photostimulus that starts after pole_out_time cannot be ruled out. Without the five sessions of the clock check, 260 of 579 (0.449) are modulated and the bin-start bootstrap mean is 9.89 ms (s.d. 11.4), inside tolerance, while the observed onset stays at 25 ms; the bootstrap mean then mixes resamples that find the early bump with ones that find the change near 25 ms. Many neurons are altered; neither the count nor the latency matches. The latency fails only with those five sessions included, and the count depends on the unit selection the files do not explain (selection_undocumented finding).
deviations: The photostimulation codes are not described in the files; codes 1 and 3 are read as early sample and 2 and 4 as early delay photo-activation, 5 and 6 as delay photo-inhibition, from the onset of the ALM response and the sessions' ogen sites (data check).

The dataset holds more neurons than the paper (676 against 454), so the count is judged; the fraction is reported.

The latency's 10 ms bins are labelled by start, centre and end, as the paper does not say which; the onset search starts at photostimulus onset. Subtracting the pre-onset change is a variant not in the paper.

outcomes.statement: Despite the changes in individual neurons, the average ALM spike rate is nearly unchanged by CN photo-inhibition (4.15 against 4.39 spikes/s).
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 9
outcomes.quote: However, the average spike rate was nearly unchanged (control: 4.15 spikes/s; photo-inhibition: 4.39 spikes/s; p=0.58, two-tailed t-test)
outcomes.notes: All 676 neurons, all trials, delay epoch: 3.379 spikes/s control, 3.767 photo-inhibition (change +0.387); unpaired t-test p = 0.214, paired p = 0.022. Modulated neurons: 4.652 and 5.780 (unpaired p = 0.069, paired p = 0.007). Correct trials give the same pattern (3.366 and 3.728; unpaired p = 0.246, paired p = 0.029). With all neurons the control rate is about 19% below the paper's 4.15 and the photo-inhibition rate about 14% below its 4.39, and both rates of the modulated neurons are above their tolerances, so the criterion's tolerance is not met under any reading; the absence of a change holds by the unpaired test and not by the paired one. The dataset holds more slow neurons than the paper's count allows (the 454 fastest have a mean delay rate of 4.89 spikes/s, against 3.36 for all 676), so the rate level depends on a neuron selection the paper does not describe. Without the five sessions of the clock check, 3.310 and 3.716 (unpaired p = 0.227, paired p = 0.031). The absence holds under the unpaired test, the one assumed (see deviations).
deviations: The photostimulation codes are not described in the files; codes 1 and 3 are read as early sample and 2 and 4 as early delay photo-activation, 5 and 6 as delay photo-inhibition, from the onset of the ALM response and the sessions' ogen sites (data check).
Putative pyramidal neurons by the width of the files' mean waveforms (E1), which gives more neurons than the paper reports; the units table has no quality field to tell which the paper left out.

Lick early trials are left out of the neural analyses (the Methods say so for performance only); a standard choice. So are trials outside the units' observation intervals (120 trials of BAYLORCD8 20171020, which hold no spikes).

Assumed: the absence test is the unpaired two-tailed t-test over neurons. The paper says only "two-tailed t-test" (main text, "control: 4.15 spikes/s; photo-inhibition: 4.39 spikes/s; p=0.58, two-tailed t-test"), and p = 0.58 for a 0.24 spikes/s change fits an unpaired test. Here the two disagree (unpaired p = 0.214, paired p = 0.022), and the criterion asks that the outcome be marked as resting on the reading when they do.

outcomes.statement: Among ALM neurons modulated by CN photo-inhibition, 108 increase and 89 decrease their responses.
outcomes.source: Results, paragraph 9; Figure 3e
outcomes.quote: Individual ALM neurons increased (108/197) or decreased (89/197) their responses during CN photo-inhibition
outcomes.notes: Of 270 modulated neurons (all trials), 158 increase and 112 decrease, both outside 108 +/- 10.8 and 89 +/- 8.9; correct trials give 137 and 86. The dataset holds more neurons than the paper, so the criterion's fraction, given for fewer neurons, does not strictly apply; the increase fraction, 0.585, is inside 0.495 to 0.605 (correct trials 0.614, just outside). outcomes.notes: The dataset holds only ALM recording sessions (54 files, 13 mice); the VGAT-ChR2-EYFP behavior mice are not in it.

findings.statement: The dandiset holds only the ALM recordings (54 sessions, 13 mice). The CN recordings (878 units in 18 mice and 60 units in 2 L7-cre x Ai32 mice), lick times, the behavior-only sessions (lesions, 1.3 s and response epoch photo-activation, 0.5 s and response epoch photo-inhibition), the VGAT-ChR2-EYFP experiments and the anatomy are not in it; 26 of the 45 claims cannot be tested.

photo_stim_id has no description, and the files hold no laser trace. The codes are 1 and 2 in fastigial, 3 and 4 in dentate and 5 and 6 in L7-cre x Ai32 sessions; from the ALM response, 1 and 3 start at sample onset and 2, 4, 5 and 6 at delay onset. Codes 5 and 6 both last through the delay; the ALM change to code 5 fades over the delay (mean absolute change 3.1 to 3.2 spikes/s early in the delay, 2.1 at its end) and to code 6 does not (2.95 to 3.00 early, 2.93 at its end), as two powers would give, but which is 1.5 mW and which 4.5 mW cannot be told, nor the photo-activation power. The ALM change to CN photo-inhibition starts about 30 ms after pole_out_time under both codes, so when the photostimulus starts relative to pole_out_time cannot be checked.
The descriptions of pole_in_time, pole_out_time and cue_time say they are relative to the trial start; the values are on the session clock (pole_in_time - start_time is 0.57 s in most trials).

Hemispheres disagree with Supplemental Table 1. The files place the manipulated CN of CD12 and CD13 on the left, the same side as the recorded ALM, where the table gives the right CN and the Methods say ALM was always recorded contralaterally; CD14 is recorded in the left ALM in the files and the right ALM in the table. Within each subject every session has the same coordinates.

Subjects anm00314746, anm00314756, anm00314757, anm00314758 and anm00314760 are named AN105 to AN109 in the paper; by site, anm00314756 is AN106 and anm00314757 is AN107, and the other three cannot be told apart. The genotype of the wild-type mice is "unknown", and session_description is empty.

The unit counts differ from the paper. By the paper's width rule the files hold 1082 putative pyramidal neurons in the 9 photo-activation mice (557 fastigial, 525 dentate) against 912 (446 and 466), and 676 in 20 sessions of the 4 photo-inhibition mice against 454 in 19 sessions. Nothing says which units or session the paper left out; the units table has no quality or isolation field (its columns are cell_type, sampling_rate, spike_times, obs_intervals, electrodes, electrode_group, waveform_mean and waveform_sd), and the paper gives no per-session counts. The files hold more slow neurons than the paper's counts allow (195 of the 676 fire under 0.5 spikes/s in the delay).

The cell_type column labels 60 units "pyramidal" whose mean waveform has a trough-to-peak width under the paper's 0.45 ms (33 under 0.35 ms), and 3 units "unknown"; the waveforms are sampled at a stated 20 kHz in every file, including the 34 sessions recorded with the 32-channel NeuroNexus probe, which the Methods say were sampled at 25 kHz (the other 20 used the 64-channel probe).

In 5 of 54 sessions the response to delay photostimulation could not be shown to be locked to the trial events (BAYLORCD12 20180125 and 20180129, BAYLORCD13 20171211 and 20171215, anm00314756 20151023), mostly sessions with few units or photostimulation trials; the other 49 show it. Leaving them out changes no outcome.

In BAYLORCD8 20171020 the behavior runs on after the recording ends. The units' observation intervals end at 7221.8 s, and the last 127 of 462 trials, from 7223.1 to 8481.4 s, hold no spike of any unit. The obs_intervals column records this correctly, but an analysis that does not apply it counts those trials as silent (this attempt's first run did, which lowered the photo-inhibition sessions' mean rate).

disagreements.reason: ALM meets the criterion only when the response epoch fixes the preference (cell 28). With the sample or delay epoch the maximum falls at -0.45 to -0.05 s, so the result depends on that reading, against the paper's "qualitatively similar". The CN half is not in the data. Problem 4: neurons are also selected (E2) on the same correct control trials that later give the held-out selectivity, so selection inflates the sample-epoch "CI above 0" test.

Cell 32: latency 14.7-22.1 ms (bootstrap mean, any bin label or trial set), outside 3.3-10.9 ms. The count, 267 of 676, is outside 197 +/- 19.7; only the fraction, 0.395, falls inside its 10% band. Problem 1: the dataset holds more putative pyramidal units than the paper, so the "fewer neurons, judge the fraction" fallback was applied when the data in fact hold more neurons. Problem 6: the photostimulus onset relative to pole_out_time was never checked, and the fig3d latency depends on it.

Cell 34: no reading has both rates in tolerance (all neurons 3.23/3.65; modulated 4.41/5.62, the second outside 3.95-4.83). The paired test differs (p = 0.010). Problem 1: the extra units are also a plausible cause of the low mean rate in fig3e (3.23 vs 4.15).

Cell 36: counts 158/109 (all trials) and 136/84 (correct) are outside 108 +/- 10.8 and 89 +/- 8.9. The increase fraction 0.592 is inside 0.495-0.605 on all trials, but the fraction fallback strictly applies only when the data hold fewer neurons, and they hold more (676 vs 454).

Cell 41: latency is in tolerance with the bin-start label (2.1-5.1 ms), but the modulated fraction, 0.25-0.32 (137-178 of 557), is far below 0.509 +/- 0.051 and the count 227 +/- 22.7, under both windows and both trial sets.

Cell 58: selectivity is within tolerance (62.1%) only with independent trials and squared ratio. Variance is within (24.0%) only for single-trial activity, a dimension the notebook added; it chose trial-type means as its main reading, and those give 34.2%, outside 22.8-31.2. Problem 3: both are defensible readings of "task-related activity", so the outcome rests on which one is accepted.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: The full executed notebook of the author-revise-1 run (commit 106c4290e5), with its conclusions and summary, the helper module, the claims file, the attempt record and the README, with the paper under paper/. Report, transcripts/gao-2018/verifier-2-report.md. Besides the per-claim points, it found two findings without printed output behind them (the BAYLORCD8 20171020 end of recording and the 25 kHz sampling of the 32-channel recordings) and loose numbers in the photo_stim_id finding; the data check now prints the obs_intervals end and the trials after it (cell 6) and the stated sampling rate per probe type (cell 5, 34 sessions with the 32-channel probe at 20 kHz), and the findings give the printed numbers.

disagreements.reason: The outcomes entry says outcome reproduced; its own verification response says "Changed from reproduced to partially_reproduced", and cell 81, the Summary and the README all say partially reproduced. The numbers support partially reproduced (cell 80): under the chosen reading (independent trials, trial-type means, squared ratio) the selectivity is 62.1%, inside tolerance; the variance is 34.2%, outside 22.8 to 31.2%. The assumed: true flag and its stated assumption are correct and reasonable.

paper_notes.statement: For the population selectivity of Fig. 2c (E3), which epoch fixes each neuron's preferred trial type, and are the 10 preference trials 10 in all or 10 of each type? On these data the epoch decides whether the maximum lies in the response epoch (response epoch) or just before the go cue (sample or delay epoch); the paper says only that the epoch gave "qualitatively similar preparatory activity", which holds here. For Fig. 3f the random draw of the preference trials matters as much as the trial count; in the last 500 ms of the delay, 15 of 20 draws (5 of each type) and 13 of 20 (10 of each type) bring ALM selectivity under CN photo-inhibition to zero.

For the latencies (Extended Data Fig. 9a, used for Figs. 3 and 4), which time labels a 10 ms bin (its start, centre or end), is the onset searched from photostimulus onset, and is a pre-onset baseline subtracted? The labels shift the latency by up to 10 ms, and without a baseline the dentate latency comes out near 0 ms.

For the fractions captured by the cd (64.1% of selectivity, 27.0% of variance), are they measured on the trials that estimated the cd or on independent trials, is the fraction of RMS or of squared RMS, and is the variance that of single trials or of trial-type means? Only one combination of these matches both numbers here.

entries.title: A cortico-cerebellar loop for motor planning (Gao et al. 2018)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Gao, Davis, Thomas, Economo, Abrego, Svoboda, De Zeeuw and Li (2018) that can be tested on dandiset 000007, which holds the ALM recordings of 13 mice during CN photo-activation or photo-inhibition. It tests ALM selectivity, the effects of CN photostimulation on ALM neurons and on the coding direction, and the behavior of the recording sessions. The lesion, CN recording, licking, VGAT-ChR2 and anatomy data are not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Gao et al. (2018) from dandiset 000007
